articles.headline: Jose Ramirez has completely changed Guardians' playoff story in 48 hours
keyFacts: The Cleveland Guardians defeated the Chicago White Sox 9-5 on Thursday to tie the American League Division Series at two games apiece.
Cleveland third baseman Jose Ramirez hit a two-run home run and drove in three runs to help force Game 5.
The series winner will be decided in Game 5 on Saturday, with the victor advancing to face the Tampa Bay Rays.
body: The Cleveland Guardians appeared to be running out of answers. Two losses against the Chicago White Sox had pushed Cleveland to the brink of elimination in the American League Division Series. The Guardians needed someone to change the direction of their postseason.
Jose Ramirez decided to take that responsibility.

Cleveland defeated Chicago 9-5 on Thursday night, forcing a decisive Game 5 after trailing the series 2-0. And for the second consecutive evening, Ramirez played a starring role. The veteran third baseman homered and drove in three runs Thursday, continuing a remarkable turnaround at the most important moment of the season.
Ramirez delivers another enormous postseason moment

The Guardians trailed 2-1 entering the fifth inning when Ramirez faced Chicago reliever Jordan Hicks. Ramirez connected on a 99.9 mph fastball and sent it into the right-field seats for a two-run home run. The blast gave Cleveland a 3-2 lead and briefly silenced the crowd at Rate Field. It was an especially impressive swing considering the velocity of the pitch.
JOSÉ RAMÍREZ! GUARDIANS JUMP IN FRONT! https://t.co/setZbLqz5I
— MLB (@MLB) October 9, 2026

According to MLB.com, the 99.9 mph fastball was the fastest pitch Ramirez had ever homered against. It also tied the fastest pitch hit for a postseason home run by a Cleveland player during the pitch-tracking era. The home run was only part of Cleveland's offensive response. After Chicago regained the lead, the Guardians erupted for six runs in the sixth inning. Jo Adell delivered a two-run single during the rally, helping Cleveland take control. Patrick Bailey also homered in the victory.
Cleveland's season comes down to one game
The turnaround has been remarkable. Chicago won the first two games of the series in Cleveland, putting the Guardians in a position where one more defeat would end their season.
Instead, Cleveland won consecutive road games by scores of 9-3 and 9-5.

Ramirez has been central to that reversal. His recent performances have been particularly encouraging after a season complicated by wrist surgery and offensive inconsistency. Now the Guardians return home with momentum and an opportunity to complete the comeback.
Game 5 is scheduled for Saturday at 8 p.m. ET in Cleveland. The winner advances to face the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Championship Series.
Cleveland still has plenty of work remaining. But the Guardians have already accomplished something significant. They turned a seemingly hopeless series into a winner-take-all showdown.
And Ramirez has reminded everyone why he's one of baseball's most dangerous October performers.

articles.headline: Could Trump play hardball to prevent an MLB lockout?
keyFacts: President Donald Trump said he wants to intervene to help prevent a potential Major League Baseball lockout.
MLB owners demand a hard salary cap to address payroll disparities, which the players union strongly opposes.
A potential owner-imposed lockout looms when the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1.
body: LOS ANGELES — For baseball fans, excitement about the World Series is tempered by the increasing likelihood of a work stoppage in the sport soon after. President Donald Trump says he can prevent it.

Trump said Sept. 26 at a college football game he would like to stave off a Major League Baseball lockout before the Dec. 1 expiration of the owners’ current collective bargaining agreement with players. The sides are miles apart on owners’ insistence that a salary cap be imposed to prevent runaway player salaries. It’s a demand players adamantly oppose.

“I would do it if it was appropriate,” Trump said in an interview with conservative radio host Clay Travis at the Texas-Tennessee game. “I would certainly do it if I could. Baseball looks like it could have a strike. If it does, it would be too bad. It is tremendous — if you look at sports, it seems the baseball players and owners do the least well. They’re going to work it out the same way as they do in all other sports. But if I could help, I’d love to help.”

For many, Trump’s comments are fanciful at best, in the category of his claims to have ended multiple foreign wars and conflicts. Trump, in these boasts, portrays his administration’s foreign policy as uniquely effective at stopping global bloodshed.

Trump said he would like to avoid a Major League Baseball lockout before the Dec. 1 expiration of the owners’ current collective bargaining agreement with players. (Erica Denhoff/Icon Sportswire via Newscom)

In reality, he can fully or even realistically take credit for ending the long-running feud between Armenia and Azerbaijan, longtime rivals in a mountainous geographic region that acts as a natural bridge between Eastern Europe and Western Asia . Trump hosted a historic peace summit on Aug. 8, 2025, at the White House, where Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan signed a joint declaration to end decades of conflict.

Still, Trump could throw the prestige of the White House into averting a baseball work stoppage. He could muster public pressure, political sway, or the use of executive agencies such as the National Labor Relations Board to, in theory, impose a settlement. And if the Nov. 3 midterm elections go poorly for Republicans, as polls suggest is the case, Trump could be looking for a conversation-changing win that would make him the political savior of America’s national pastime.
A seemingly intractable dispute

MLB’s current collective bargaining agreement is set to expire a bit over a month after the end of the late October conclusion of the World Series. A potential owner-imposed lockout looms with the two sides so far apart on a range of issues.

Most prominently, owners want to introduce a hard salary cap and floor system, similar to the NFL, NBA, and NHL, citing payroll disparities and a need for competitive balance. Smaller-market owners contend they don’t have the revenue to keep up with some teams’ large spending on player salaries, such as the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets.
While the Mets haven’t won a World Series since 1986, the Dodgers currently dominate baseball. The Dodgers have won two straight World Series titles and three over the last six.

Los Angeles outfielder Kyle Tucker earns an average of $60 million annually and $240 million total. Los Angeles two-way player Shohei Ohtani’s contract is worth $700 million over a decade. (Jeff Chiu/AP; Frank Franklin II/AP)

On a recent sunny day at Dodger Stadium, as the team awaited its National League Division Series opponent, the Atlanta Braves, fans taking tours of the ballpark were confident of their team prevailing for a third straight title. Los Angeles is led by players earning deep into the eight figures annually, including outfielder Kyle Tucker and two-way player Shohei Ohtani.
The MLB Players Association strongly opposes any cap. The union argues that a spending floor for low-spending teams is the real solution rather than restricting player salaries.

The idea is to compel teams to spend on fielding a quality team, capable of competing for a World Series championship. Take the Milwaukee Brewers, operating this year with a payroll roughly between $128 million and $153.4 million, depending on player benefits and calculations. That places the team well under a proposed $171.2 million minimum. If such a salary floor were adopted, the Wisconsin-based team would be forced to increase team spending by roughly $20 million to $40 million to meet the new threshold.

If Trump entered the fray in a bid to fend off a baseball work stoppage, he wouldn’t exactly come to the table as an objective party. He has publicly sided with MLB owners in their push to establish a hard salary cap.
“If you don’t have a salary cap, you don’t have a sport,” Trump said June 5 while speaking to reporters on Air Force One. “They should have done it a long time ago.”
The president added it was “shocking, frankly, that they didn’t put a cap on many years ago.”
Trump, in his second, nonconsecutive term, has frequently tried to exert influence on sporting matters.
“I know so much about sports,” Trump said at one point during his June 5 exchange with reporters, in which he also addressed the college sports landscape and the NBA Finals.

In baseball, Trump previously claimed credit for improving the chances that the late Pete Rose would be inducted into baseball’s Hall of Fame. Rose, the all-time hits leader who died in 2024 at 83, was banned from baseball for betting on the sport.
Mixed record of presidents, in office and out, settling baseball labor disputes
Whatever Trump’s views are on the labor issues that threaten MLB’s 2027 season, legally, the president can’t force either side to do anything.

Presidents have been able to use some legal measures against workers’ strikes in the past. But those have usually been temporary tools to intervene in industries such as ports and steel, which can send the nation spiraling economically if not resolved.
MLB is a billion-dollar, privately run league. So, the president can’t compel opposite sides of baseball negotiations to do anything.

Not that previous presidents haven’t tried. The last time the two sides seriously fought over the possible introduction of a cap system, in 1994-95, the players went on strike for 232 days. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series, President Bill Clinton attempted public mediation.

Clinton appointed a special mediator and called both sides to a high-profile White House summit. But his efforts ultimately failed to broker a voluntary deal. The strike only ended on April 2, 1995, after U.S. District Judge Sonia Sotomayor, now a Supreme Court justice, issued a preliminary injunction against what she called the owners’ unfair labor practices, forcing a return to previous labor terms.

Nearly a decade earlier, an ex-president was able to stave off a baseball-related dispute. Former President Richard Nixon acted as a binding arbitrator in October 1985 to settle a compensation dispute between the league and the MLB Umpires Association.

Nixon’s intervention came at what turned out to be the height of sorts in his public comeback attempts after resigning the presidency over Watergate on Aug. 9, 1974. In May 1986, Nixon made the cover of Newsweek , with the headline, “He’s Back”. The story focused on Nixon’s postpresidency rehabilitation, detailing how he worked to transform his public image from a disgraced president into an elder statesman and recognized foreign policy expert.

When the current MLB labor agreement expires, Trump will still have more than two years left in the White House. But a precedent of the late Nixon averting a baseball-related strike could loom large in efforts to save the 2027 season.
DEMOCRATS FEAR EARLY VICTORY TALK COULD MAKE VOTERS COMPLACENT AND HAMPER TURNOUT

Trump and Nixon once shared a long-standing relationship of mutual admiration. Trump, as a celebrity businessman in the 1980s, frequently corresponded with Nixon. And though their White House stints were separated by decades, the presidential pair have shared a common sense of grievance regarding the media.

Negotiating a baseball-related settlement could get added to the Nixon-Trump commonality list. Though with modern-day owners and players so far apart, it’s unclear if Trump’s usual hardball approach to politics would work.
David Mark ( @DavidMarkDC ) is the managing editor of the Washington Examiner magazine.

articles.headline: NBA title race heats up as Knicks defend crown against a revamped field
keyFacts: The 2026-27 NBA season begins October 20 with the New York Knicks defending their championship title.
Contenders rebuilt their rosters, with Philadelphia adding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, and Miami acquiring Giannis Antetokounmpo.
The season opens on October 20 with matchups including the Knicks hosting Philadelphia and San Antonio hosting Oklahoma City.
body: Source: Kelleher Photography/Shutterstock.com The 2026-27 NBA season opens with a rare mix of continuity and major change. The New York Knicks are defending their first championship since 1973, while the San Antonio Spurs are coming off a Finals appearance. Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo, LeBron James and Jaylen Brown have all moved into new championship situations.

The Oklahoma City Thunder also remain firmly in the picture after posting the league’s best regular-season record last year. With the regular season beginning Oct. 20, several teams have legitimate reasons to believe they can reach the NBA Finals.
The Knicks have a champion’s foundation

New York enters the season with something every contender wants: proof that its core can win four playoff rounds. The Knicks went 53-29 during the regular season before finishing the 2026 playoffs 16-3 and defeating San Antonio 4-1 in the Finals.

Jalen Brunson remains the central offensive figure, while Karl-Anthony Towns, Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby give the roster several ways to attack and defend. NBA.com noted that New York’s offense actually became more efficient during its championship run, reaching 119.9 points per 100 possessions in the playoffs.

The challenge is repeating that level of postseason execution. Mitchell Robinson is no longer available, and the Eastern Conference has added more competition. Still, the Knicks return a proven starting group and have already shown they can handle pressure when the stakes rise.
The Spurs have unfinished business

San Antonio has perhaps the clearest motivation among the Western contenders. The Spurs went 62-20 last season, finished second in the West and reached the NBA Finals before losing to New York in 5 games. Their young core now has direct experience of basketball’s biggest stage.

Victor Wembanyama is the centerpiece. The 7-foot-4 forward-center combined improved offense with elite rim protection last season, and San Antonio also has rising guards Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper. De’Aaron Fox adds another established playmaker to the mix.

That combination gives San Antonio multiple sources of creation while keeping Wembanyama at the heart of the defense. The bigger question is whether the young roster can turn the lessons from a Finals loss into another deep run. The Spurs will have plenty of attention from the opening weeks.
Source: Victor Velter/Shutterstock.com The Thunder still have championship-level pieces

Oklahoma City enters the season after another dominant regular season. The Thunder finished 64-18, the NBA’s best record, while Shai Gilgeous-Alexander won his second straight MVP and earned another First Team All-NBA selection.

Chet Holmgren and Jalen Williams give Gilgeous-Alexander two important running mates. Holmgren averaged 17.1 points, 8.9 rebounds and 1.9 blocks last season, while Williams remains a versatile scorer and defender when healthy.

Their biggest test is already clear. San Antonio eliminated Oklahoma City in 7 games in the Western Conference Finals, ending the Thunder’s attempt to return to the Finals. That matchup could become one of the defining Western Conference rivalries if both teams maintain their trajectory.
The Nuggets still have Nikola Jokić

Denver remains dangerous for the simplest reason: Nikola Jokić is still running the offense. The 3-time MVP helped the Nuggets produce the NBA’s top offense last season, and his career true shooting percentage of 64.1% ranks first among players who have averaged at least 18 points per game.

Jamal Murray also enters the season after a major offensive step forward. He played 75 games last season and averaged a career-high 25.4 points while posting a 62.2% true shooting percentage. Aaron Gordon provides another important piece when available.

Denver’s concern is balance. The Nuggets ranked 21st defensively for the second straight season, and several rotation pieces departed during the offseason. DeMar DeRozan joins the group, while Denver hopes improved health and new defensive options can address its biggest weakness.
Source: gints.ivuskans/Depositphotos The 76ers built a star-heavy lineup

Philadelphia may have the most dramatically reshaped contender. Jaylen Brown arrived after averaging a career-best 28.7 points for Boston last season, while LeBron James joined Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and promising young guard VJ Edgecombe.

The talent is obvious, but fitting those pieces together will be the central storyline. Maxey provides speed and shot creation, Brown adds two-way strength, James remains an elite passer and scorer, and Embiid gives Philadelphia an interior focal point when healthy.

That makes availability and chemistry crucial. Philadelphia went 45-37 last season and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals, so the new roster must translate its individual talent into postseason consistency. The opening matchup against the defending champion Knicks will provide an immediate measuring stick.
Miami added a former MVP centerpiece

Miami changed the Eastern Conference landscape by acquiring Giannis Antetokounmpo from Milwaukee. The 2-time MVP now joins Bam Adebayo, creating a frontcourt built around elite defense, transition play, and interior pressure.

The Heat also added Klay Thompson, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Bobby Portis, giving the roster additional shooting and championship experience. Last season, Miami generated transition opportunities on 24.9% of its possessions, the highest rate tracked by Synergy over its 22 seasons.

The obvious question is how Miami creates enough half-court spacing around its two frontcourt stars. Thompson, Hardaway and Andrew Wiggins can help, but the Heat will need their new pieces to fit quickly. Antetokounmpo’s first official game comes Oct. 21 against Minnesota.
Source: zhukovsky/Depositphotos Boston and Cleveland can disrupt the East

Boston enters a different phase after Jaylen Brown’s departure . JBoston enters a different phase after Jaylen Brown’s departure. Jayson Tatum remains the team’s primary star, while the Celtics added Paul George and Mitchell Robinson. Boston went 56-26 last season, finished second in the East and lost in the first round of the playoffs. Detroit finished first in the Eastern Conference with a 60-22 record.

Cleveland offers another established threat. The Cavaliers went 52-30 and reached the Eastern Conference Finals before being swept by New York. Donovan Mitchell received a four-year extension, while James Harden re-signed for three years, keeping Cleveland’s main veteran pieces together.

Those teams give the East considerable depth behind New York, Philadelphia and Miami. Boston has experience and new veteran talent, while Cleveland has continuity and an established core. Their presence could make the conference race especially difficult to predict once the postseason matchups take shape.
The season could create several major playoff clashes

The NBA schedule points toward a packed opening stretch. The Knicks host Philadelphia on Oct. 20, San Antonio hosts Oklahoma City the same night, and Denver visits Oklahoma City on Oct. 22. Those games will quickly introduce several of the league’s biggest storylines.

The calendar also includes an early showdown between Miami and Minnesota on Oct. 21, when fans will see Giannis Antetokounmpo make his Heat debut. Golden State visits the Lakers that night, while Cleveland travels to Philadelphia on Oct. 22.

The championship race will ultimately be decided months later, but the ingredients are already visible. A defending champion, two recent Finals teams, an MVP-led Thunder squad and several radically rebuilt rosters give the NBA a deep group of plausible contenders.
TL;DR
The Knicks enter as defending champions after a 16-3 postseason run.
San Antonio returns after reaching the 2026 NBA Finals behind Victor Wembanyama.
Oklahoma City brings back an MVP-led core after finishing 64-18.
Philadelphia and Miami made major moves by adding LeBron James, Jaylen Brown and Giannis Antetokounmpo.
Denver, Boston and Cleveland add more proven talent to an already crowded championship picture.

articles.headline: Iran's Houthi allies step up deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia
keyFacts: Three Saudi citizens were killed in an Iran-backed Houthi attack targeting Riyadh's main airport, Saudi civil aviation authorities said.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran revised its proposals to initiate peace talks with the United States through mediators.
President Trump stated that the United States will not attack Iran before the upcoming midterm elections on November 3.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Three Saudi citizens were killed Thursday in an attack by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Riyadh's main airport. Fighting between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen has escalated this week in what appears to be the new epicenter of the wider .

- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that Tehran had revised its proposals to initiate peace talks with the U.S. and stood ready to finalize them through mediators. President Trump rejected a "7-day plan" offered by Iran in late September to get both sides back around the negotiating table.

- The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, eased Friday to around $103 a barrel after Mr. Trump promised the U.S. would not resume attacks on Iran before the U.S. midterm elections early next month. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he offered no specifics.
Saudi authorities say 3 civilians killed in attacks on Riyadh airport claimed by Houthi rebels

Three Saudi citizens were killed and several other people "of different nationalities" were wounded in attacks targeting Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a Saudia Airlines aircraft, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said Friday.

Thursday's attack was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since the kingdom and allied forces in neighboring Yemen launched a major military offensive last weekend aimed at retaking territory seized by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
It was a significant escalation in what appears to be the new epicenter of the wider war in the Middle East sparked by the joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran in late February.

The first attack Thursday afternoon targeted airport facilities, while the second struck the aircraft, which was empty at the time, the Saudi statement said. It did not identify those responsible, though the Houthis have claimed to target the airport repeatedly this week with ballistic missiles, including on Thursday.

Among the dead was Capt. Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, the Saudia Group said in a statement seen by the Associated Press. It appeared to be the first confirmed attack on the Saudi national carrier since the new offensive against the Houthis began.
The Saudi aviation agency, GACA, said in its statement that injuries to citizens and people of other nationalities "ranged from minor to serious."
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they have declared a theater for military operations.
On Wednesday, Saudi officials said attacks on the Riyadh and Abha airports claimed by the Houthis had killed three people.
CBS/AP
Iran says it has revised proposals to renew peace talks with U.S.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that Iran had revised its proposals for negotiations with the United States and was ready to finalize them through intermediaries.

"We have made our revisions to these proposals. Once they are finalized, we are supposed to sit down through the mediators and consolidate them," Pezeshkian said during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
He said Iran had put forward proposals, and the U.S. had also presented new ones, but he accused Washington of repeatedly scuppering diplomatic efforts.
"Every time we hold talks with the U.S., they attack again," Pezeshkian said.
Addressing Putin, Pezeshkian thanked Russia for its positions on regional issues, including at the United Nations.

"Our efforts are aimed at ending the war and ensuring that the rights of the Iranian people are respected within the framework of international law," Pezeshkian said. "But if the United States seeks to proceed through unilateralism, it will not be possible."
USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego for first time in over 10 months
The and its more than 4,500 sailors returned home to San Diego on Thursday for the first time in 321 days, a jubilant homecoming after a long deployment that included months in the Middle East.

Braving the heat, hundreds of family members and friends waited for hours in the sun to greet their loved ones. As the ship pulled into the harbor, a roar of cheers erupted from a pier. Sailors stood at attention on the deck for the aircraft carrier's long approach, and after they were released, smiles and waves broke out as sailors took out their phones to call people on the pier.
In one such reunion, McKenzie Adkins held her 10-week-old son Declan as she waved to her husband, Alexander, on the ship's deck, before the new father met his son for the first time.

The Lincoln carrier strike group had been deployed for , including more than 250 uninterrupted days at sea this year. Much of that time was spent in the Middle East, where the aircraft carrier and its escort ships supported the U.S. war against Iran. It left the region in late August.

U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia issues new security alert over airport attacks

The U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia is warning Americans to "exercise heightened vigilance" if they are traveling through King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh due to attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militant group.

"The Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including against civilian airports, and the military conflict has the potential to escalate," the embassy wrote on X. "U.S. citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."

The Houthis have launched attacks on the airport, hundreds of miles into interior Saudi Arabia, four times this week. Three people on Oct. 6 and 7 in Saudi Arabia, including one at King Khalid International Airport, according to the country's aviation authority.

The embassy had already warned citizens not to travel near the Yemeni border. U.S. government employees are banned from traveling within 20 miles of the border. On Thursday, the embassy also said government officials now require special authorization to travel through King Khalid International Airport.
Trump says U.S. won't attack Iran before midterms, touts oil coming through strait

President Trump has promised the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, which take place on Nov. 3. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.

The Trump administration has consistently provided numbers for the millions of barrels being escorted out of the Strait of Hormuz under U.S. military protection. Moving out 22 million barrels of oil in one night would mark a total similar to prewar levels.

articles.headline: Trump cuts $810 million in federal spending he previously approved
keyFacts: President Donald Trump cut $810 million in previously approved federal spending, primarily targeting aid for undocumented immigrants and refugees.
Bipartisan lawmakers criticized the cuts, with Senator Susan Collins calling the action an illegal usurpation of Congress's appropriations powers.
Private groups have filed lawsuits, and Congress may restore the funding as part of a future spending deal.
body: President Donald Trump recently snipped $810 million in federal spending. The late September cuts would come to spending authorized mostly for federal aid to undocumented immigrants.

“President Trump is committed to utilizing all possible tools to cut wasteful and harmful government spending that does not benefit American citizens,” a White House spokesperson said in a Sept. 25 statement . The Department of Health and Human Services experienced the most cuts. The president removed $28 million in HHS research funds and $10 million from the agency’s Office of Minority Health. Trump also nixed $567 million in grants that would have gone to charitable and nongovernmental organizations aiding refugees.

Other agencies also had their dollars trimmed. Unsurprisingly, the Education Department, which Trump is downsizing, experienced the second-largest cut at $95 million, followed by the Department of Housing and Urban Development at $56 million. The departments of Commerce, Homeland Security, Justice, and the Treasury each had their funding reduced by $9 million to $15 million.
Some legislators in Congress are aggrieved at the president’s action.

“Trump is taking the bipartisan funding that we passed, funding the Democrats and Republicans agreed on that he signed into law, and he’s now ripping out the pages he doesn’t like,” complained Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA), her party’s top member of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
(Washington Examiner illustration; Tom Brenner/AP; Getty Images)

Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) sought to block the cuts by introducing legislation and pressing the chamber to pass it promptly. He was unable to muster sufficient support in the chamber, and his effort faced obvious hurdles: a GOP-controlled House and the president’s veto.
Democrats were not the only legislators complaining.
“I think it’s wrong, and I think it makes it very difficult for Congress to do their job,” observed Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD), who sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee.

The spending that Trump deleted was part of a larger bill that Republicans and Democrats had bargained for and that the president himself had signed into law. The pocket rescission, then, feels like a betrayal to some legislators. Congress has just two months to pass spending bills to keep the government open, and Trump’s action likely will make Senate Democrats all the more wary of cutting deals with Republicans.

Aside from the politics, the use of a pocket rescission is legally dubious. Rounds noted that the Constitution doesn’t provide a president with a line-item veto, and the pocket rescission “is almost the same thing.” Congress attempted to empower the president with a line-item veto in 1996. The Supreme Court struck down the law two years later after then-President Bill Clinton was sued for using it. The court reasoned that an alteration to a previous spending law must go through the Constitution’s lawmaking process, which requires both chambers to approve it and the president to sign it.

Last month’s action is the second time Trump has deployed a pocket veto. In September 2025, he nixed $4.9 billion in spending on international aid programs. Various groups sued the administration, but the Supreme Court decided by a 6-3 vote that the plaintiffs likely lacked standing to sue, while cautioning that its decision “should not be read as a final determination on the merits.”

Trump could have chosen a clearly legal path to attempt to rescind the funds. As this magazine reported last year, the 1974 Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act permits a president to ask Congress for permission not to spend funds. The executive may send a message to the Senate and House specifying the funds to be cut, and Congress has 45 days to pass a bill to approve the president’s request. The rescission fails if both chambers do not pass the rescission bill within that time frame. Indeed, Trump partnered with Congress to lop $9 billion from foreign aid programs and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting in the summer of 2025.

This time around, however, the president chose to deploy a pocket rescission, which requires no congressional action to take effect. He and the Office of Management and Budget waited to deliver his request for cuts until five days before the end of the current fiscal year. With the House of Representatives recessed and its members out campaigning across the country, it would have been all but impossible for both chambers to vote to pass the cuts before the funding expired.

“This move shows that OMB intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law,” Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) wrote in a social media post. “Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also, it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers. OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”
Collins, who helms the Senate Appropriations Committee, has vowed to “address these illegal actions.”

The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office issued a legal opinion in 2018 stating that, constitutionally and legally, there is “no basis to construe the ICA as a mechanism by which the President may, in effect, unilaterally shorten the availability of budget authority by transmitting rescission proposals shortly before amounts are due to expire.”
SCHUMER’S GRIP ON NEW YORK LOOSENS UNDER TRUMP 2.0

The GAO sent a letter to Congress after Trump’s latest pocket rescission. The agency declared the 45-day clock extends past the end of the fiscal year to Nov. 9, and that Trump’s letter to Congress was not legal grounds for him to continue to withhold the money.

Whether Trump will be forced to spend the funds to be restored is unclear. Various private groups have filed lawsuits against the pocket rescission. Congress also may restore the funds as part of the broader fiscal 2027 spending deal it is working on.
Kevin R. Kosar ( @kevinrkosar ) is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and edits UnderstandingCongress.org .

articles.headline: In open source cybersecurity, AI is kind of a problem — but it can also be a solution
keyFacts: IBM's Jamie Thomas said vulnerability disclosures are rapidly rising while the time required for cybercriminals to exploit them has shrunk to minutes.
AI-generated bug reports have overwhelmed open-source projects and companies, forcing Google to temporarily suspend its vulnerability rewards program.
Thomas proposed using AI-powered tools to filter out fake reports and help developers fix vulnerabilities more efficiently.
body: The last few years have seen a growing wave of vulnerability disclosures heading towards the cybersecurity industry, and the people working on fixing these flaws are often struggling to keep up. And while AI is a major contributor to this problem, but also an essential part of the solution.

Speaking at the recent Linux Foundation Open Source Summit, Jamie Thomas, IBM's Chief Client Innovation Officer for Enterprise Security, warned there is “a bit of a tsunami in vulnerability disclosures,” with approximately 66,000 unique entries expected to emerge in 2026 alone.
At the keynote, titled The Future of Open Source Security in the Age of AI, Thomas stressed this represents a fourfold increase compared to seven years ago.
So, how can the cybersecurity industry possibly keep up with this pace, Thomas asked, especially when the expectations placed on developers and security professionals continues to grow?
The answer seems to be the same as with everything these days - AI.
Attackers are moving faster than ever

The volume of attacks is definitely an issue, but it’s not the only issue. Cybercriminals are also a lot faster at exploiting them, giving defenders an ever-shrinking window to identify and remediate different security issues.
Citing publicly available data, Thomas said the time required to exploit a vulnerability shrunk from days to as little as 29 minutes.

“And in fact, we're seeing a rapid increase in cyberattacks, as well as malware attacks,” she said.

For businesses that rely heavily on open source, this is definitely cause for serious concern. A vulnerability in a widely used component can potentially affect hundreds, if not thousands, of downstream applications and businesses. To add insult to injury, cybercriminals don’t really wait for the cybersecurity community to publicly disclose a vulnerability before they can exploit it.
“We're seeing the time to exploit is actually negative,” she said. “Many times we're getting a disclosure and we don't have a patch yet.”

That is the position the defenders are in, right now. They are expected to respond to a rapidly growing number of security issues in a shrinking timeframe, while attackers take advantage of automation to accelerate their operations.
AI is making life harder for open-source maintainers
And then, along comes AI for the sucker punch.

Sure, AI-powered tools are capable of identifying vulnerabilities and improving software security, but they are also more than effective when it comes to creating a pile of inaccurate, duplicated, and otherwise unactionable vulnerability reports.

Where does that leave open source maintainers, you might ask? Large companies typically have dedicated security teams, and even those struggle with an influx of low-quality reports, as you’ll see below. Many open source projects, on the other hand, are maintained by small groups of devs, sometimes even by a single individual.

Earlier this year, the developers of curl, the popular open-source command-line tool and software library, terminated their HackerOne bug bounty program, saying the financial incentives had people submitting poorly researched, and sometimes entirely fake, reports. The influx, which included AI-generated submissions, was simply unmanageable for the project’s security team.

Even the almighty Google bent the knee, recently being forced to temporarily suspend its Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program following a significant increase in invalid and irrelevant reports (many of which were AI-generated, apparently). As of October 1, 2026, the company is no longer accepting new submissions and will reassess the program in early 2027.

Even Linux creator Linus Torvalds complained about the problem, recently saying AI-powered bug hunters have made the Linux security mailing list "almost entirely unmanageable." He criticized the enormous duplication of reports, saying different researchers were using the same AI tools to identify vulnerabilities that were already fixed, or at least reported.
IBM wants AI to become part of the solution

So what’s the solution? According to Thomas, the security community should not abandon AI-powered vulnerability discovery but should instead use the same technology to help maintainers handle the growing workload.

This is where the Linux Foundation’s Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) initiative, could step in. A collaboration between tech firms, developers, and the wider open-source community could allow OpenSSF to strengthen the supply chain security, and for IBM, the priority is now to reduce the burden on maintainers. That can be done by making vulnerability management more efficient and that, in turn, can be done with AI-powered tools filtering out duplicate and bogus reports, assessing the severity of different bugs, and identifying issues that need urgent attention.

AI can also help remediate issues, help developers understand vulnerable code, suggest fixes, and evaluate whether patches introduce additional problems. This is an important caveat, since some earlier reports found the majority of AI-generated remediation suggestions caused more problems than they solved.

articles.headline: How to complete To the Skies in Arc Raiders
keyFacts: Players must collect four specific arc parts including Arc Performance Steel and Pop Trigger to complete the To the Skies quest in Arc Raiders.
Players need to scan a crashed Arc Probe and an Arc Courier, which can be found across various maps.
The quest is completed by repairing and activating the Gondola Prototype located east of the eastern Spaceport elevator using the gathered materials.
body: ⚡ You'll need Arc Performance Steel, Pop Trigger, Arc Thermo Lining, and Arc Synthetic Resin.
⚡Scan a crashed probe and courier then repair the Gondola Protoype east of the east Spaceport elevator and activate it.
Arc Raiders' To the Skies quest involves finding a few arc parts to repair one of the Prototype Gondolas being used to shuttle raiders to Pendola Pass.
First things first, to complete To the Skies you're going to need a variety of arc parts:
- 1x Arc Performance Steel: Salvaged from big arcs like Bastions, Bombardiers, Leapers, or Baron Husks.
- 1x Pop Trigger: Salvaged from small exploding Pop robots or couriers.
- 1x Arc Thermo Lining: Salvaged from Pops, Fireballs, or Baron Husks.
- 1x Arc Synthetic Resin: Salvaged from intact Arc Probes or Baron Husks.
There are a number of other ways to get the materials above, generally by salvaging arc enemies, so if you don't have one of each yet, keep your eyes peeled.

The first step is to scan a crashed Arc Probe and an Arc Courier. These spawn on almost every map, but your best bet is the Electromagnetic Storm condition. To scan them, simply interact with the icon at the head of each.
Repairing the Gondola Prototype

After this, you'll have to find and repair the Gondola Prototype on any one of four maps—I did it on Spaceport, so that's the one I'll show you. Grab those listed arc materials and head to the spot above, just east of the eastern exfil elevator, north of Communications Tower and south of East Plains Warehouses.

There, you'll find the Gondola Prototype resting on its side on some crates by a raider structure. Now just install those four parts and interact to activate the Gondola Prototype and complete the quest, though you might want to back away from it a bit.

articles.headline: Critical Role Just Gave a Controversial Answer to D&D’s Most Important Question
keyFacts: During episode 37 of Critical Role’s Campaign 4, Dungeon Master Brennan Lee Mulligan repeatedly intervened to help player Sam Riegel's character, Wicander Halovar, survive an assassination attempt.
Mulligan gave Riegel a choice to reroll a failed death saving throw with disadvantage in exchange for freeing a demon companion from a magical contract.
The author stated that while altering rules to prevent character death can cheapen the stakes, adding narrative consequences to such decisions represents a balanced storytelling approach.
body: People sit around a table to play a game of Dungeons & Dragons to have fun. Heroic deeds, exciting adventures, and hilarious moments are all part of the experience — but so is death. The risk of player characters dying adds important stakes to a D&D story, but because it feels terrible to have your character die as a player, that makes it very difficult for Dungeon Masters to navigate that aspect of the game. The latest episode of Critical Role’s Campaign 4 proves this.

Episode 37 of Campaign 4, “Death to Tyrants,” is all about character death. Without going too much into the details of the campaign’s complex plot, one of the characters, Wicander “Wick” Halovar (played by Sam Riegel), is the target of an assassination attempt orchestrated by his family. The entire episode consists of four long combat rounds in which Riegel’s character gets downed (reduced to 0 hit points or less) multiple times as his friends try to save him. However, there comes a moment when Wicander’s fate seems sealed as Riegel fails one last death saving throw.

DM Brennan Lee Mulligan’s decision at that moment was interesting, to say the least. It made me reflect on how hard it is for a DM to balance the “fairness” that should be present in a D&D game with the natural impulse to preserve a story and its characters, making sure everybody goes home happy. What is the best way to handle character death, especially if that character is important to the story?
Brennan Lee Mulligan didn’t want Wicander to die

Watching the episode, it seems Mulligan was trying to give Riegel every advantage possible to make sure Wicander survived his ordeal. At the beginning of combat, Wicander was hit by a Hold Person spell (cast by his own sister!), which is a nasty way to start. The spell inflicts the Paralyzed condition, meaning that every attack hitting the target from within five feet is a critical hit. Once a character is downed, critical hits cause them to automatically fail two death saving throws; after three failed saves, the character is dead for good.

Hold Person requires a Wisdom saving throw when it’s cast. If the target fails, they roll again at the end of each of their following turns to try and break free from the spell (from 5th edition onwards, D&D tends to be more lenient with this type of spell). When it came to Wicander’s first turn after being hit with the spell, Mulligan suggested that Riegel could delay his turn (an action that no longer exists in the 5th edition rules or in the 2024 update but remains a common house rule). Doing so would allow Halandil Fang (Liam O’Brien) to grant Bardic Inspiration, adding a bonus d8 to the next Wisdom save.

Leaving aside the “delay your turn” house rule, this was an unusual call from Mulligan. When a character is Paralyzed, they also have the Incapacitated condition, meaning they can’t take any action, bonus action, or reaction. So, there is nothing to delay, and ruling the opposite defeats the purpose of the Hold Person spell. It’s a bit of a grey area in the rules, but I would rule against it as a DM.

Later in the episode, Mulligan did something even more egregious. Wicander was dying again and on his last death saving throw. Riegel rolled, and even with the extra help coming from another Bardic Inspiration, he failed. Farewell, Wicander! It made for a shocking moment, but nothing unusual for Critical Role. Travis Willingham’s character, Teor Pridesire, also died a few episodes ago.

Yet Mulligan gave Riegel a second chance. He asked if Riegel wanted to reroll that last death saving throw with disadvantage (rolling twice and taking the lower result) or help Tyranny, the character played by Whitney Moore, by breaking her contract. Tyranny and Wicander have had a strong bond since the beginning of the campaign. She is a demon, bound in service to Wicander by a magical contract. If Wick dies, Tyranny’s contract will default to the evil head of the Halovar household, Yanessa. So, Riegel was given the choice of risking it all or accepting death while saving his closest friend from a terrible fate. He chose the former and managed to pass the death saving throw despite the disadvantage.
Should DMs try to avoid death in D&D?

This is a moment most DMs can identify with. When a player character dies in one of our games, there is always a temptation to use some kind of deus ex machina to undo it. But what do you sacrifice when you're unwilling to sacrifice a player? Every D&D game is meant to tell a story, and a good story is one where the stakes feel real, especially in the context of an emergent narrative where every decision and dice roll can shape the outcome. Making players feel invincible can potentially make them lose interest in the story, and thus in the game itself.

While not every DM will agree with Mulligan’s decision, there is something to learn from it. He gave Riegel a tough choice, after all. His chances of success with that new roll with disadvantage were about 30%. Moreover, if he failed, he wasn’t just losing Wicander; He was also causing a bad outcome for his friend. If a DM decides it’s correct to “undo” death at the table, I believe this is the right way to do so: by adding more stakes to the story to make up for the loss caused by this form of interference.

It is a bit odd that Mulligan did not give Willingham the same chance. In episode 30, “Here in the Dark,” Teor Pridesire was felled by the undead in Obrimus Manor, without any DM shenanigans trying to save the burly Paladin. Perhaps this is because Teor was accompanied by an NPC (his brother Cyd) rather than a player character, giving Mulligan no inspiration for a meaningful storytelling moment like the one between Wicander and Tyranny.

Towards the end of “Death to Tyrants,” Wick went down yet again after being hit by two attacks. He blocked one with a use of Shield, but the other brought him down to negative hit points. Then, Brennan asked Riegel if he wanted to retroactively “take back” the Shield — thus going down to two failed death saves again — to free Tyranny from her contract. This felt like an excess. Sure, it threw all the players into distress, and it was fun to see Riegel fidget with the choice for a while, but it was also clear that Mulligan was trying to steer the story in a certain direction. Riegel opted to free Tyranny, which gave her the chance to use Aid on Wick and give him advantage on his next saving throw, ultimately leading to his survival.
Death is an important element of D&D games

As D&D evolved over time and editions, character death has become more uncommon; between death saves and resurrection spells, it’s hard for a character to truly kick the bucket. If Wicander’s party had a single member with the Revivify spell prepared, for example, all the drama seen in “Death to Tyrants” would have been instantly nullified.

D&D characters are more than some stats on a sheet. Often, they feel real, and losing them hurts a lot for players. It’s understandable that DMs sometimes pull their punches to create a more pleasurable experience for everyone. Still, balance is one of the most important qualities a DM should strive for. To help players feel immersed, you want the world to feel real, and to do that, death has to be part of the equation. Forcing a character to survive, especially if it’s done for story reasons, can cheapen the looming threat of potential death for everyone at the table, ultimately damaging the immersion and the overall experience of the game.

What to do when death comes knocking in D&D is a tough decision. Mulligan showed an interesting example in Critical Role, but every DM should act according to their preferences and the shared understanding at the table. Discuss this eventuality with your players at the start of the adventure: as long as everything is clear and you all have fun by the end, there are no wrong choices.

articles.headline: Labour fends off the Green party in closely watched UK by-election
keyFacts: Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali won the parliamentary by-election in Holborn and St Pancras, defeating Green Party leader Zack Polanski.
The victory boosts Prime Minister Andy Burnham after Labour previously lost left-wing support to the Green Party.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski said he will stay on as leader despite facing criticism over a party motion about Zionism.
body: The Labour Party has won an election for a parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer, fending off a challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for the British prime minister.

Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of the local council, won the seat in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras with 12,292 votes, compared with 8,928 for Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader who came second.

The victory, which had been expected, will buoy Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was recently installed by lawmakers fearful that Starmer’s unpopularity was opening the way for a challenge by the populist Reform UK party at the next national election.

After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour looks to have won many voters back, a result that triggered more questions about Polanski’s leadership, who had promised to make his party “an eco-populist” movement.
The Greens have drawn some voters away from Labour. There are now five Green MPs, compared with one in 2023.
But Polanski, 43, came under fire after party members passed a motion declaring that Zionism is racism at their annual conference.

The move, which called for “the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine” was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party lawmakers. Polanski did not vote on the motion.
Labour has held Holborn since the seat was created in 1983.
Labour’s Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the United Kingdom as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for “those who seek to divide us”.
“We have a responsibility to defend what we’ve built and pass it on,” she said.
After conceding defeat, Polanski, who is not an MP, answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader, and described the result as part of “Andy Burnham’s honeymoon”.
Polanski congratulated Abdi-Wali, but said, “One in three voters backed us here, and we know that many more considered it.”

Al Jazeera’s Sonia Gallego, reporting from London, said, “The constituency has been going through what some people have been calling ‘the Burnham bounce‘ … so far there is a deep sigh of relief (for Labour) that they’ve managed to hold on.”
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has changed voter habits. The Greens, far more critical of Israel’s conduct than any other party, got a boost in the 2024 general election.
Back then, Starmer won the seat with 49 percent. Andrew Feinstein, a pro-Palestine independent candidate, came second, with 19 percent.
Polanski has raised the “progressive vote” while “reducing the Labour vote”, he said.

body: - Published
Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name.

The series will pick up events after the end of the hit film, with Constance Wu and Henry Golding playing their lead roles of Rachel and Nick, while Ronny Chieng is back as Eddie and Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh will have a recurring role as Nick's mother Eleanor.

"It's a 'Crazy Rich' family reunion!" said Adele Lim, who co-wrote the film, calling it the sequel we've been waiting for". It will "delve into the characters and worlds of Kevin Kwan's brilliant books" over eight episodes, she said.
The show will be made by HBO, and the news was announced days after HBO's parent company Warner Bros announced its Â£110bn (Â£82.8bn) merger with Paramount Skydance.
Adapted from Kwan's bestseller books, written between 2013 and 2017, the film topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes.
It featured an all-Asian cast and told the story of an Asian-American woman who gets a culture shock meeting her boyfriend's ultra-wealthy family in Singapore.
Lim is showrunner for the new TV series and will be one of the executive producers, as will the the film's director Jon M Chu.
He said the film had "changed his life", calling the cast and crew the "most creative and hilarious group of people I've ever known".
"Since then, this cast has become movie stars, superheroes, arena-filling performers and even an Oscar winner, so bringing everyone back together feels like coming home."
Lim added: "Our writers room is humming and we can't wait to share what we've come up with."
The series, co-produced by HBO and Warner Bros Television, will start production next year.

"Constance, Henry, Ronny, and Michelle are global superstars, and we know the passionate fans of the film and megahit novels can't wait to see more," said said Casey Bloys, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance Direct-To-Consumer.

The Altruists, covering the rise and fall of FTX, will start streaming on November 19.

On November 19, Netflix will start streaming The Altruists, an eight-episode mini-series based on the rise and fall of cryptocurrency exchange FTX. The streaming service has released a trailer for the show, featuring its stars Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried and Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison. In the trailer, you'll see how the two of them had met and of the times Ellison's "all in" mentality had supposedly influenced how they ran their business.

Bankman-Fried founded FTX, which offered crypto exchange and crypto hedge fund services, with Gary Wang. FTX originally formed inside Alameda Research, a trading firm co-founded by Bankman-Fried and Ellison, who eventually entered a romantic relationship with each other. They reportedly bonded over "effective altruism" and believed that high-income jobs are worth taking if the end goal is to give income away to charities.

FTX was once one of the world's largest cryptocurrency changes with a daily trading volume of $10 billion until its rapid collapse in 2022. The price of its native token took a nosedive and a lot of users withdrew their money, fearing a liquidity crisis. That led to the revelation that $8 billion of its customers' money had gone missing. In court, Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried directed her to use FTX customer funds to buy property, make political donations and fund Alameda Research. Bankman-Fried was found guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy in late 2023 and was sentenced to 25 years in prison. He recently tried to appeal his fraud conviction, but an appeals court had denied it.

body: The upcoming anime adaptation of Sony's Ghost of Tsushima just took another big step forward, with Crunchyroll revealing more details on the cast and crew attached to the project, as well as a 2028 release window.

articles.headline: Antarctica’s penguins are sending us a distress signal
keyFacts: A study found that the world's largest chinstrap penguin colony on Zavodovski Island declined by two-thirds since 2011.
British Antarctic Survey scientists said climate disruption is the likely cause and warned it increases the risk of ecosystem collapse.
Researchers stated that chinstrap penguins may need to be classified as an endangered species due to accelerating population loss.
body: Chinstrap and macaroni penguins nesting on the volcanic slopes of Zavodovski Island. | Nicole Richters via British Antarctic Survey
This story was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed. Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.

“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, professor Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey .

The Guardian reported in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem. The new study, published on Wednesday in the journal Current Biology , indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird — which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek — may need to be classified as an endangered species.

Zavodovski Island had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.

Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic Peninsula to 5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity Peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4°C, about 20°C above normal for the time of year — a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy.”

Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the northwest of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.

Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30 percent — though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.

He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”

The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.

Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “ Penguin Pompeii hypothesis ” of a sudden population fall, this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

articles.headline: Mike Collins fends off claims he’s a ‘bigot,’ rips ‘trust fund kid’ Jon Ossoff in Georgia Senate debate
keyFacts: Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Congressman Mike Collins traded personal attacks during a Georgia Senate debate on Thursday.
Ossoff accused Collins of bigotry, while Collins denied the charges and criticized Ossoff's background and campaign donors.
The latest RealClearPolitics polling average shows Ossoff leading Collins by nearly eight percentage points in the Senate race.
body: Rep. Mike Collins was accused of being a “bigot congressman” while Sen. John Ossoff was derided as a “trust fund kid” bankrolled by an associate of Jeffrey Epstein during Thursday night’s fiery Georgia Senate debate.

“Mike Collins has brought dishonor to our state through his personal bigotry and his widely documented ties to white nationalists,” Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent, charged in his opening statement in the first of several personal attacks leveled by both candidates.
The senator repeatedly suggested his GOP opponent was racist and antisemitic – invoking varioussocial mediascandals involving the congressman, his staff and his son-in-law.

“[Y]ou’ve hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office, and you have promoted neo-Nazi content online,” the senator later claimed, accusing Collins of being “in cahoots” with white supremacists.
The Republican congressman insisted in response that “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don’t care where the source is.”
“And I tell him that too,” added Collins, seemingly referring to his son-in-law David Alan Scheer II, who allegedly shared anti-Jew and white nationalist rhetoric on social media.
“It’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.”
Meanwhile, Collins took aim at Ossoff’s support of far-left candidates and his receipt of campaign contributions from lefty billionaire Reid Hoffman.

“I’ve never heard him say a word about his DSA pick up there [in Michigan] … Abdul El-Sayed. Hasan Piker? How about Reid Hoffman? None of those. He doesn’t denounce anybody or anything or condemn them because he’s part of them,” Collins charged.
“One of his megadonors is data center billionaire Reid Hoffman, who is also one of Epstein’s buddies,” the congressman said.
“He’s got an answer to those people. He doesn’t have to answer to local people.”
Collins also attacked the senator’s opposition to President Trump’s tax-cutting agenda and his role in the fall 2025 government shutdown.
“Tax cuts are the answer to keeping more money back in people’s pockets … but my opponent doesn’t get that,” Collins said.
“My opponent’s a trust fund kid who’s never had a job in his life. He doesn’t understand that. He doesn’t understand business.”

The congressman also noted that “it was just this time last year, that Jon Ossoff shut the government down for 48 days. He shut it down, y’all. Right when we were trying to get that emergency money out for Hurricane Helene so that our farmers and our small communities could repair and prepare for this year’s harvest.”
“He didn’t care about that,” Collins argued. “He shut it down because he wanted to defund Border Patrol and ICE … we deserve to know why he left that border wide open.”
The latest RealClearPolitics average of polls shows Ossoff with a nearly 8 percentage point advantage over Collins in the closely watched Senate race.

articles.headline: Live-action Cyberpunk 2077 film reportedly in development, with CD Projekt Red collaborating with Paramount to make it
keyFacts: A live-action Cyberpunk 2077 film is reportedly in development in collaboration between CD Projekt Red and Paramount Pictures.
CD Projekt Red joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski stated on X that the company is excited about partnering with Paramount.
CD Projekt Red stated they have no further details to share at this time regarding the project.
body: UPDATE 12PM BST: CD Projekt Red seems to have confirmed the partnership and film, with joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski commenting on X that: "We're excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise. We look forward to sharing more details at the appropriate time."

ORIGINAL STORY 11:40AM BST: A live-action Cyberpunk 2077 film is reportedly in the works at Paramount Pictures. Producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura - a former Warner Bros. exec influential in signing the The Matrix and Harry Potter films, and known for producing the Transformers films - is said to be attached to the project, with CD Projekt Red collaborating.

The report comes from Deadline, though the publication had no further information to share than what's above. CD Projekt Red told us it doens't have anything to share beyond what Nowakowski said on X.

Believing that CD Projekt Red would venture into live-action film territory doesn't take a stretch of the imagination. The company's Netflix anime partnership on Cyberpunk Edgerunners has been a success, with a second series due to air this month, on 20th October. The first season, released in 2022, was "fantastic", Wes wrote in his Cyberpunk Edgerunners impressions article, and amassed considerable Netflix viewing figures.

Live-action adaptations of video game-based series are also becoming increasingly popular, with The Last of Us and Fallout particularly finding wide success. CD Projekt Red being involved with the Cyberpunk 2077 adaptation would also somewhat heal a wound left by not being involved with The Witcher Netflix adaptation. CD Projekt art director Pawel Mileniczuk called this a "missed opportunity" when I talked to him for a Witcher 3 10-year anniversary article last year.

Meanwhile, CD Projekt Red is working on Cyberpunk 2, a project that's in pre-production, but with an expanding team - close to 200 people as of 31st July 2026 - full production doesn't seem far away. The sequel apparently adds a second city alongside the iconic Night City setting, and it's described as being like "Chicago gone wrong".

Should the live-action film prove real, and be made, the questions are what story will it tell - the same as in Cyberpunk 2077? - and which actors will play the game's well-known roles? The most famous of those roles is Keanu Reeves' portrayal of Johnny Silverhand, a character who used Reeves' likeness in the game. Could Reeves star in a film adaptation?

Cyberpunk 2077 was released in 2021, and its rocky launch has since become infamous. But CD Projekt Red did extensive work improving the game after release, focusing its efforts around a kind of 2.0 relaunch alongside the game's "remarkable" Phantom Liberty expansion, in 2023.
Paramount, meanwhile, recently acquired Warner Bros., and has since reorganised into mega-company Skydance. Activision's former leader Bobby Kotick has been employed on the board of it.

articles.headline: Man City titles 'absolutely not' tainted - Maresca
keyFacts: An independent commission found Manchester City guilty of the majority of 115 Premier League financial charges.
Manager Enzo Maresca said the club's titles are not tainted and reiterated his complete trust in the owners.
Manchester City has appealed the verdict, and the team is preparing to play away against Liverpool on Sunday.
body: - Published
Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says the club's titles are "absolutely not" tainted after they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.
Maresca reiterated his faith in the club's owners and belief that they will win their appeal against the verdict during a news conference on Friday dominated by questions on the matter.
The Italian, notably relaxed as he offered his responses, rejected the suggestion City's titles have been tainted by the ruling, as he knows "exactly the effort that the club put in to achieve" them.
An independent commission found Manchester City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
The club have appealed against the verdict and claimed in a statement the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Preparing to play their first match since that verdict was announced, away to rivals Liverpool on Sunday, Maresca said in an in-house interview on Thursday the "feeling is fantastic" among his players and they are not affected by "the noise" surrounding the club.
He added on Friday: "The reason I joined this club is that I completely trust, 100%, the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don't have doubt about that.
"I spoke with the club for sure. We all trust, and probably the right moment to speak about that is when we are going to win this appeal."
He added: "For me, the players - we can control just the pitch side, the football side. So we are focused on that. This is what we can do and what we can control."

Appointed as Pep Guardiola's successor in June, Maresca is in his third spell at the club following time spent with the academy and as Guardiola's assistant coach - including during the Treble-winning 2022-23 campaign.

The 46-year-old has won each of his first five Premier League games in charge of City, and could become the fourth manager to win his first six of a spell in charge of a club in the competition at Liverpool on Sunday.

The announcement of the verdict reached by an independent panel, which found City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m, means Maresca's side will expect to receive an even more hostile reception than usual at Anfield.

Asked if he had any concerns over the atmosphere during the match, Maresca said: "It will be a tough game, for sure. We need to be ready, the focus needs to be about the game, but we know the environment at Anfield.
"It probably will be worse because of the situation but, again, it will be our duty to do our best and try to win the game.
"The reason I decide to become manager is for this type of game."

Maresca thanked one journalist who asked a question not related to the verdict, confirming talisman Erling Haaland is "ready" to play against Liverpool after recovering from his efforts for Norway during the international break in Marbella.
More on Man City charges
Maresca would not confirm whether he has read the independent commission's findings.
The former Leicester City and Chelsea boss said the charges against the club were not discussed during his conversations about taking the job in the summer.
And he insisted he would "100%" have still accepted the role had the findings been published before an agreement was reached.
"We didn't speak about that because I don't think it was a problem for the club at the time and I think they are are thinking in an honest way," Maresca said.
"I think they are convinced that in the end we are going to win the appeal."

Earlier on Friday, Bayern Munich manager and former Manchester City captain Vincent Kompany said: "I played 11 years for the club and I've loved all the years I've played for the club. Everything we've achieved and done on the pitch I'm really proud of.
"Everything else, as a player you're not a part of that. Right now, as a coach of Bayern Munich, I'm not too occupied with that topic."

articles.headline: US Attorney calls out 'loud-mouth' California Dems as feds step in with Skid Row drug bust: 'They're lunatics'
keyFacts: Federal and city authorities executed 28 arrest warrants and 44 search warrants during a drug crackdown in Los Angeles' Skid Row neighborhood.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli criticized California Democratic politicians for watering down state criminal laws and reducing deterrence.
The operation targeted members of multiple gangs, including the Crips and Bloods, who Essayli said keep homeless people addicted.
body: First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli called out California Democrats for watering down the state's criminal law after federal law enforcement led the charge on a massive drug crackdown in the infamous Skid Row neighborhood on Thursday.
Essayli told Fox News Digital in an interview that California's state and local law enforcement have worked with the feds just fine, but that it's the politicians who are getting in the way.

"Unfortunately, states like California have totally watered down their laws, their criminal justice laws. They've also emptied their prisons and closed prisons, so effectively, there's not much of a deterrence on the state side. No one faces any serious consequences on the state side," Essayli said.
NEWSOM BLASTED BY SHERIFF IN HIS OWN BACKYARD OVER CALIFORNIA CRIME AS VICTIMS CRY FOUL

"We work really well with our local law enforcement partners," he continued. "Local law enforcement isn't the problem. It's more the governor, it's the legislature, it's these loud-mouth federal, you know, Congress members who all they care about is attacking the administration, attacking the president."
Essayli did give credit to Mayor Karen Bass for approving the Los Angeles Police Department to participate in Thursday's Operation Save Skid Row.
KAREN BASS GRILLED OVER BROKEN HOMELESSNESS PROMISE, BLAMES BUREAUCRACY FOR SLOWED PROGRESS

"This is a climate in which you have people right now trying to defund the police . You have people trying to disarm the LAPD, and those people are on the side of criminals," he added. "Anyone who's calling for disarming the police is on the side of the drug dealers that we arrested today. They're lunatics."
Operation Save Skid Row saw federal and city authorities execute 28 arrest warrants and 44 search warrants in an effort to dismantle drug distribution networks in the notorious neighborhood.
TALARICO PUT ON DEFENSE AFTER 2020 COMMENTS ABOUT DEFUNDING POLICE RESURFACE: 'WE MUST REPLACE'

Over 100 law enforcement vehicles were involved in the operation, with arrests targeting members of multiple gangs, including the "Main Street Crips," "Grape Street/Raymond Avenue Crips" and the "Pueblo Bishop Bloods."

"We are no longer going to have open-air drug markets in the United States, let alone on Skid Row. And that is the reason you see so many homeless people who are experiencing psychotic episodes, who are unwell, they aren't seeking help, it's because you have people, like the drug dealers we are arresting today, keeping them addicted and taking their public assistance money to pay for their drugs," Essayli said during a news conference on Thursday.
