articles.headline: A national verdict on Trump 2.0 is coming. Nine midterm voters share where they stand
keyFacts: The Guardian launched a voter panel interviewing nine US citizens across the country about key political issues.
Millions of Americans will vote on November 3 to decide control of the House, Senate, and 36 governorships.
The Guardian reported that reporters will return to interview the voter panel before final votes are cast.
body: US voters are about to deliver their first national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.

Today, the Guardian launches its 2026 midterm voter panel. Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about the issues that matter to them, from the cost of living, immigration and healthcare to the war in Iran and whether they trust their political leaders.

The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood with less than a month to go until election day. The Guardian will return to its voter panel before the final votes are cast.
What’s the most significant issue for you in the midterm election?
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

So, I’m an economics student, and one of the things I’ve noticed more and more is, we work more, but we seem to be getting further and further behind. Why is it that my grandfather could work an eight-hour union job and have enough to take care of five or six kids, and yet I work the same job and I’m struggling to get by? That makes no sense to me. I don’t understand why so many CEOs are saying companies are making record profits while people have to have two and three jobs.
Yajaira Martinez 43; Pharr, Texas; independent/disaffected Trump voter

My biggest hit that I’m having right now is labor. I don’t have labor. I don’t have workers that can, you know, finish the houses as fast as we used to. It causes a ripple effect when it comes to supply and demand – houses taking longer, interest rates going higher, so everything is just going up in value.
Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal

It would be likely ICE. I feel like that right now is having the largest, most powerful negative impact on people in this country. And it’s very blatant, and I feel like stopping that would be a good touchstone for how we all move forward.
What do you think is the most significant thing Donald Trump has done in his second term?
Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

His recent deal to establish or re-establish American hegemony in Greenland is a really big deal. Making sure that America has access to Greenland, and China does not, is a very important thing that Donald Trump has done. Also, with the Iran war, it is very important what we’re doing there, and I hope for as quick and decisive a success as can possibly be reached.
Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive

I’m going to say the assault upon not only the immigrant community, but every community that he sees as being vulnerable. Giving the American people or a certain sector within the American population permission to be cruel and to exalt in this public display of cruelty – we are going to spend a long time recovering from that.
Morgan Akin 85; Redding, California; Democrat/moderate

There’s a number of things, but destroying public structures, buildings and so forth in Washington DC, and then building new ones that have no relevance whatsoever to democracy or the people of the country. He is benefiting from his office, increasing his income [by] billions of dollars, while Americans are suffering with high gas prices and food prices and so forth. I just filled my car up, just before you called. I have a Honda CRV, which is not a big car, and it cost me $78 to fill it up.
Does your life feel better or worse than it did two years ago?
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

My life is better. Myself and my husband, we are both retired. I’m retired from the education field. I was clerical; I was not in a teaching role. My husband was assembly line. He was a blue-collar worker. He worked for General Motors. But I’d say that we’re better off because I feel safer. I feel more hopeful for the future. The economy, of course – things could be better with gas prices, but I think that that’s a temporary problem right now.
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

Economically, much worse. It’s worse than it was two weeks ago. I have a pickup truck. Filling my gas two weeks ago, two months ago, was $80. Now, it’s $120. I’m expecting it to be $150. And not only that, is my [utilities] bill going to go up. What else is going to go up? Groceries are going to go up just because shipping is going up. I’m not getting a raise yet, again, we’re making record profits. Who are those profits going to? Not you and me, not the people who need the money.
David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive

My parents went out of business during Trump 2. My parents started a business, like, 20 years ago in the auto industry. They were very, very lucky because neither of them have college degrees. What sort of started in Trump’s disastrous Covid response, that was one of the first times that my parents had to take out a big loan that they weren’t sure about. In their industry, the tariffs have completely shaken up everything. It has caused them to have a lot less certainty, and eventually that built up, and they couldn’t go on any longer. They’ve got a new business in the works. We’re doing OK, but that was something that did personally affect me.
Patti Fucci 46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderate

I never thought, in 32 years, as a Venezuelan American, that I had to carry my passport with me everywhere I go. I never thought that I will live in fear in the United States, even though I’m an American citizen.
How optimistic are you about America’s future?
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

I’m very optimistic. This country’s been through worse and she’s always came out on top. I don’t think that there’s a better country in this world. I don’t think there’s a more powerful country in this world. As far as the best in leadership, I think we have it. As far as goals and policies that this country should strive for, I think Donald Trump has those in place.
Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal

I’m not very optimistic. Thirty years ago, I would have said yes. We were the shiny new penny that everybody loved after World War II. Now we see the reverse: European countries have gotten their footing and are passing us. China is the worry. Xi is a smart man, a benevolent dictator. If we continue down this path of electing the Trumps of the world who do not embrace science, education or long-term economic stability and infrastructure, this country will continue to decline.
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

Oh, I think America’s future is behind it. I believe we’re starting to witness the collapse of the American empire, sad to say, but just understanding how economics work and how everything is based on the petrodollar. I understand why Trump wanted to get away from EVs [electric vehicles], because if EVs took over, then less oil would be needed and the US dollar would be needed less and less. But what good is being the richest person on an ash heap? All the water is dehydrating. As the earth gets hotter and hotter, water is not sitting on the planet’s surface anymore, it’s in the air. It’s just going to be more storms, more lakes drying up, and what’s going on right now? Oh, we need all the fresh water for datacenters. What do you need datacenters for if nobody’s going to be here?
Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive

I take great encouragement from some of the voices of the Black community, the immigrant community, people who have been involved in activism for decades – I do have optimism. It’s hard to balance sometimes, because there are certainly times when I feel like, oh, who even cares? And why is our country so special that we wouldn’t fall down the hellscape of authoritarianism? But there is a large movement, there is a large resistance, and it’s growing week by week. And I think we have a long tradition in this country of believing that we do have rights. We have these incandescently beautiful founding documents.
David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive

I see movements domestically – obviously, the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] that has been killing it in the primaries. They’ve already done more damage than the Tea Party or Occupy Wall Street ever did, and it feels like this is just the beginning. So I’m very, very optimistic, and I think the world that we can accomplish, a world where everyone’s needs are met, at least in the wealthiest nation in the history of the planet.
How do you want the Iran war to end?
Yajaira Martinez 43; Pharr, Texas; independent/disaffected Trump voter

Let’s be realistic: war is created for money to be created. I just feel everything just needs to end. Everybody, every country, needs to focus on themselves, and the United States needs to focus on the United States’ people.
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

I want it to end with the least amount of death. I’m a mother of five children. I have three sons and two daughters. I have one grandson. I don’t want any kind of war because war brings death. But I think that the person that’s able to end this conflict is in leadership today.
Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

I don’t think a peace deal can be reached with the existing regime. Regime change in the Middle East has been very hard to master, so it really would have to be a move of the people in Iran. The propaganda war may be the most important front for a truly lasting peace to be achieved.
Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal

At this point, we just need to walk away. There’s no winning; they are winning. We need to cut our losses and move on. I’m a little shocked that with our trillion-dollar military, one little country like Iran has somehow managed to deplete our resources. To reasonably manage a war and win, we have shown ourselves incapable. At this point, to save face, we need to spin some PR and walk away.
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

I’m a veteran, so I’m trying to choose my words very carefully on that. With the conviction of Donald Trump. With the conviction of Benjamin Netanyahu of war crimes. With the conviction of Pete Hegseth.
How do you think the war has affected perceptions of the US around the world?
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

When you have a leader that is confident in his ability and he says what he means and he means what he says and he leads with confidence, I think people respect that. So I think that we’re being respected a lot more than we were in the last administration.
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive

You know how a lot of families have those old, racist grandpas that you just leave in a corner and you don’t bring them to family gatherings? That’s who the US is right now. It’s sad, but I don’t know who our allies are. And the allies Trump has have been the enemies of the United States for generations.
Patti Fucci 46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderate
No good … We roll a red carpet for [Putin]… for [Xi Jinping] a week or two ago. We are doing business with [Delcy] Rodríguez in Venezuela, who is a criminal dictator.
What do you think about changes in the Democratic party?
Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

The most concerning section, especially in this election cycle, is that democratic socialist alliance. What they seem to be fighting for isn’t just a better safety net; it has become the dismantling of America as a concept, the dismantling of the west as a concept, and of reality itself as a meaningful concept in public discourse.
David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive

I think what’s going on in the Democratic party is very productive. I think even the hard conversations over ‘DSA outsiders’ and: ‘Are these extreme ideas what we stand for?’ I think it shows that we’re expanding the conversation to policies that will help people’s lives in a real material way, and that we don’t have to only stop the worst of the Trump administration. We can also make healthcare work significantly better for everyone in the country. That’s a real consideration.

What’s the way that we can actually win and hold on to what’s most important? I think we’re seeing that there’s a route that we can both win more and hold on to our values. The whole basis of the logic that shifts the Democrats right is that ‘at least it’s what’s good for elections’ or ‘at least we’ll win, and then we can think about all the considerations and all the reform afterward. But first we have to win.’ Well, Kamala didn’t win, so what now? Plenty of moderate Democrats did not win. Hillary didn’t win. That logic is not as sound as they think it is.
Can you imagine a Democrat in the White House in 2028? Who would it be?
Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

I am going to be in the air force. The president is the commander-in-chief of the armed forces of the United States, and as such, I will serve him honorably. If that’s a Democrat, then I will serve a Democrat honorably, because he will still be my president – or she.
Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive

If I imagine a Democrat in the White House in 2028, being elected in 2028, inaugurated in 2029, I have to make the assumption that a lot of things take place that are no longer guaranteed. Trump has been threatening the midterm elections. If a Democrat were to be inaugurated in 2029, the popular resistance needs to hold firm and ramp up its pressure. There are some solid people out there. Adam Kinzinger, he’s solid; he was a Republican, but he’s kind of gone over, gotten over that. I have a lot of respect for Pete Buttigieg, probably because he’s able to speak very cogently, very decisively, with people who disagree with him.
Patti Fucci 46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderate
Let’s not talk about 2028 until after [the] midterms. I think Andy [Beshear] and Gavin Newsom will be my two top choices if I were to think about 2028 right now, which I’m not.
Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal

This country doesn’t vote for Democrats because they love Democrats … It’ll be because Trump has ruined things so poorly, and made things so bad, that people will turn around and come back again and vote again, just like they did when Trump was in office the first time and elected a Democratic president. Now, who it is … that’s the joke in the room. Because our best candidates are those who a lot of the American public are racist or bigoted against. I’m a Mayor Pete [Buttigieg] fan. I think he’s brilliant, he’s a brilliant man, he is. Just mentally, historically, in terms of what he’s accomplished in his lifetime, he’s brilliant. He’s gay. Can he win?

articles.headline: Forza Horizon 6's first major expansion will pull up in January, now Playground Games just need to offer any kind of hint whatsoever as to what it'll look like
keyFacts: Playground Games announced that the first major expansion for Forza Horizon 6 will release on January 21st, 2027.
The developer stated that further details regarding the expansion's theme and content will be shared closer to its launch.
A second expansion is also planned to be released at a later date.
body: Forza Horizon 6 has, as is standard for the live-service racing series, settled into a steady rhythm of revolving weekly to-do lists and a gradual drip feed of fresh cars since it came out in May. Unless you're hopping on for regular bouts of driving with mates or just dig the grind, odds are most folks will have dipped in and out over the months, possibly only returning when a new season adds the likes of a drift attack mode to the open world. Horizon 6's first major DLC's likely to change that at least for a little while, and Playground Games have now revealed it'll be arriving in January.

Ever fans of catchy names, Playground are calling this opening Horizon 6 expansion "the first Premium Expansion for Forza Horizon 6" for now. It'll release on January 21st, 2027, and will be automatically granted to players who've bought the racer's premium edition, premium upgrade or expansions bundle. Those who've not already splashed that extra cash will have to buy it separately.

As for what it's themed around or entails, all the studio have said thus far is more details will be coming "closer to availability". They have at least noted that a second expansion will also be coming at some point further down the line. I'll be honest, I never got around to buying Forza Horizon 5's expansions. Both the Hot Wheels add-on with GTA 5-esque sky tracks and the Rally Adventure add-on seemed to get rather mixed reviews right out of the gate, a mark they both still sit at on Steam as of writing.

It might largely have been more of what the base game did well, but I recall having a good time with Forza Horizon 4's Fortune Island expansion. A fresh corner of the map to explore that's got some interesting scenery, flowing roads to master, and fits with the established vibe better than someone unloading a child's toybox across Mexico. Ideally, Horizon 6's get something similar with one of its expansions, which are also a good chance to put out a new area that perhaps feels a bit more concentrated in its unique Japanese vibes, rather than meandering a bit into a more standard Forza atmosphere when you're on a road that isn't right next to a key landmark.
Regardless, better DLC than its predecessor will be needed if this latest entry's to remain worthy of the bestest best sticker I gave it as part of my Forza Horizon 6 review.

As ever with games made by Xbox-owned studios, it's worth noting that the parent company behind Horizon 6, Microsoft, are subject to the BDS movement's ongoing boycott over their reported links to the Israeli military. They've also laid off thousands of people this year as part of bloodletting that's only "roughly three-quarters" of the way finished as I write this.

articles.headline: OpenAI doubles down on decision to fire three AI safety researchers
keyFacts: OpenAI fired safety researchers Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, citing a significant breach of trust regarding sensitive information.
The dismissed researchers claim they were fired for raising safety concerns, but OpenAI insists the decision was about policy violations.
The dispute comes amid growing concerns among AI staff about the safety of frontier systems and calls for companies to slow down.
body: OpenAI is standing firm on its decision to fire three safety researchers after an investigation found they committed “a significant breach of trust.”
OpenAI doubles down on decision to fire three AI safety researchers
The AI lab insisted the decision was about a ‘breach of trust,’ not raising safety issues.

In a post on X on Friday, the company said Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni were dismissed for violating “clear policies on handling sensitive information.” It insisted the decision was not about the trio speaking out about the company and their concerns about AI safety.

The post is a direct response to an open letter the researchers published on Thursday urging OpenAI to be more transparent about the decision. In it and a series of social media posts, the group said they believed they were fired for raising safety concerns and had “acted in line with OpenAI’s mission and within the working norms of the time.”
OpenAI said an internal investigation uncovered breaches “beyond what’s outlined in the letter,” but did not provide details.

The safety of frontier systems has become an increasing concern for staff inside AI companies following a series of high profile breaches this year, most notably OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face. Many staff are now calling for companies to slow down and do more to guard against the potential consequences of building self-improving systems.

articles.headline: Microsoft and Anthropic play invoice tennis with startup's $17,600 Claude bill
keyFacts: Norwegian startup Vegalabs AS ran up a $17,600 bill using Anthropic's Claude model, mistakenly believing its Microsoft Azure credits would cover the cost.
Microsoft's sponsorship rules exclude third-party marketplace models like Claude, resulting in Vegalabs' credit card being charged instead of using its sponsorship balance.
Vegalabs' waiver requests remain unresolved as Microsoft and Anthropic support teams repeatedly direct the startup to each other for billing assistance.
body: A Norwegian startup says it ran up a $17,600 bill using Claude in Microsoft Foundry after assuming its Azure credits would cover the cost. We reported a similar case in March, involving third-party model charges that weren't covered by Azure sponsorship credits. This time, the customer says Microsoft and Anthropic each directed it to the other to resolve the charges. Vegalabs AS says it received $25,060 in Azure credits through Microsoft for Startups and deployed Claude in August, expecting its analysis workloads to use that balance. However, Microsoft's sponsorship rules exclude Anthropic models purchased through Azure Marketplace. Vegalabs says Microsoft attempted to collect $16,500 from its card, with the invoiced total subsequently reaching $17,600 before tax. Vegalabs says it monitored the sponsorship portal, which continued to show available credits while separate Marketplace charges accumulated. Microsoft's Claude deployment guide says credit-only sponsored subscriptions aren't supported, but accounts with a card on file will have that card charged instead. The company says it deleted the deployment within an hour of discovering the charges. Its card issuer declined the attempted payment over suspected fraud, and $21,168 in unused sponsorship credits expired on September 8. Vegalabs acknowledges it did not read the credit exclusions or configure a budget alert. It disputes neither the usage nor the documented rule, but says the deployment interface failed to make the separate billing clear. Its request for a waiver then bounced between Microsoft and Anthropic support. The Register has seen communications from Microsoft directing the user to Anthropic. "Marketplace transactions are processed through a separate billing pipeline associated with the third-party publisher. As a result, Azure Support does not have the ability to directly waive, refund, or adjust these Marketplace charges on the customer's behalf." "If Anthropic approves the request, they can initiate the appropriate refund authorization through Microsoft." Anthropic support, however, said Microsoft did not require its authorization to process a refund and directed Vegalabs back to Microsoft. Vegalabs says four of the seven support replies it received were AI-generated, including both responses from Anthropic. It says those responses incorrectly described its account as an "Azure Student Sponsorship." We asked Microsoft on October 6 if it had any comment on the situation, but beyond an acknowledgment and a request to let us know what Anthropic had to say, the company had nothing further to share. We also asked Anthropic for its take on the situation, but the company did not respond. Microsoft's rules distinguish between credit-covered services and separately billed models offered through the same platform. Vegalabs' experience suggests that distinction needs to be clearer where customers deploy them. For now, the company has a bill and two support teams directing it elsewhere. ®

articles.headline: After Going Hands-On With the New Marvel Comics App, I Still Don't Know Why Unlimited Had to Die
keyFacts: Marvel is discontinuing the Marvel Unlimited app and replacing it with a new Marvel Comics app powered by Webtoon on November 16.
The new app offers faster release times for higher-tier subscribers and a modernized interface, though core reading features remain largely unchanged.
Marvel Unlimited will officially sunset on December 7, 2026.
body: Earlier this week, Marvel announced that it was discontinuing the Marvel Unlimited app , only to have it replaced by the new Marvel Comics app, powered by Webtoon. At New York Comic Con I had the chance to go hands-on with the app, and I am struggling to see why it needs to exist.

Just like Marvel Unlimited, the new Marvel Comics app will bring the entire Marvel and Star Wars comics libraries at both of its subscription tiers. On the surface, the big advantage Webtoon has over Unlimited is how quickly new comics will be available — with the more expensive ‘Ultimate’ tier getting new issues 30 days after print, rather than Unlimited’s 90 day waiting period.

Webtoon shared a rough roadmap for the app; it’s looking to bring in Disney and Pixar comics, make it easier to create your own custom lists, and create different profiles for all the comics readers in your home – even kids. But, Webtoon failed to share dates for when any of these improvements are coming, so at least for now, it looks like the bulk of the changes are minor cosmetic ones.

Webtoon said that its mission in designing this app was to make it faster and easier to use. After all, Unlimited has been around since 2007, and the UI still kind of looks like it’s stuck about a decade in the past. But rather than give Marvel Unlimited a facelift, the decision was made to create a brand new app. And, while the navigation does seem a bit more modernized, the app itself isn’t noticeably faster than Unlimited was. Of course, this could come down to the tablets at the Webtoon booth and spotty convention Wi-Fi, but I couldn’t really feel the difference.

Once you click into an issue, the Marvel Comics app does get a bit more compelling, though. Before you start reading the issue, it’ll bring you into a sort of overview page, where you’ll be able to see the information about the selected issue, but you’ll also be able to slide through other issues in the series on the top of the screen. There’s also a section where you’ll be able to see every reading guide that issue is a part of.

When I’m reading comics on the Unlimited app, I tend to make a beeline straight for reading guides, because I simply don’t have the patience to read entire comics runs that sometimes have hundreds of issues. Marvel Unlimited’s reading guides were excellent, and it seems like they’ve carried over to the Webtoon app. But, again, I only had a few minutes with the app in a crowded booth at NYCC, so I didn’t exactly have time to see if all of my favorite guides were intact.

Once you get into an actual comic, though, not much has changed. You can still choose between reading the entire page or reading panel by panel. With the latter option, you can also choose to have it zoom back out when you’re ready to move on to the next page, in order to appreciate all the art on the page, just the way you would in a regular comic.

That’s a great way to read digital comics, but Marvel Unlimited had the exact same options, and it wasn’t hard to set up. As nice as the new UI is, that probably could have been implemented with a hefty update, rather than asking all of the Marvel Unlimited users to move over to a whole new app. The Marvel Comics app will let you move over your library and all of your reading progress, but I can only imagine that there are going to be people who stubbornly won’t make the migration. I just hope it was worth that risk.
The new Marvel Comics app launches November 16 with more than 35,000 digital comics. Marvel Unlimited will sunset as of December 7, 2026.

articles.headline: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
keyFacts: Three former OpenAI researchers claim they were fired for raising safety concerns, while OpenAI says they mishandled sensitive information.
The former employees warned that their dismissals have made current OpenAI staff afraid to speak out about safety concerns.
OpenAI said it is finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks.
body: - Published
Three former OpenAI researchers sacked for allegedly mishandling information claim they were instead let go because they raised safety concerns at the tech firm.

"I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," Mikita Balesni posted on X, external alongside an open letter to the ChatGPT-maker, written with fellow ex-employees.
On 2 October, a spokesperson for the AI firm told the BBC its investigation "confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures".
OpenAI repeated these claims, external on Friday morning in a note from research leaders.
"We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out," the note said.
"Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment."
The dismissals come amid a growing debate over AI safety and the potential risks advanced AI systems could pose to society.
The joint letter to OpenAI leadership was written by Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, who say they were all, until recently, safety or alignment employees at the company.
Alignment is the practice of building human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

The former staff members raised concerns that their firings had made employees at the tech company "afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI".

Reposting the letter, Korbak wrote, external: "For months, I'd been raising safety concerns that we're losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave.
"I believe that was why I was fired."
OpenAI said it was finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and would announce details in the coming weeks.
"We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," Wang said in a post on X, external.
"Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of manoeuvre, I am concerned we will not be the last."

articles.headline: From Zuck to Musk: Big Tech’s Scandals and Scammers Are Coming to the Big Screen
keyFacts: Hollywood is releasing multiple movies and documentaries this fall that focus on real-life scandals and figures in the tech industry.
The films feature prominent tech figures including Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Elizabeth Holmes, and OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman.
These productions will premiere in theaters and on streaming platforms between October and December.
body: Hollywood is unleashing a handful of movies this fall, pulling the curtain back to shine a light on some of the big names in tech: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg; Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk; Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes; and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Plenty of movies have tackled themes of techno-pessimism and dug into the deep well of science fiction. Remember 2001: A Space Odyssey? Blade Runner? M3GAN? But apocalyptic threats and human-versus-machine scenarios feel much more prescient in 2026.
What’s changed is that there seems to be an appetite for Big Tech to get its comeuppance. The movies being released are real stories about the scandals and scammers affecting our daily lives.
More from CNET
The Social Reckoning (Oct. 9)

The Social Reckoning continues the story Aaron Sorkin began with the 2010 film The Social Network about Facebook. The Oscar and Emmy-winning screenwriter stepped behind the camera to helm the movie, which he once again wrote.

The Social Reckoning highlights the societal damage caused by Zuckerberg’s social media empire. Based on thousands of leaked documents from former Facebook engineer Frances Haugen, the movie draws inspiration from the 2021 Wall Street Journal article The Facebook Files, which documents the whistleblower’s actions and the subsequent fallout.

Succession star Jeremy Strong now plays Zuckerberg (Jesse Eisenberg played the bright-eyed college student 16 years ago). The film also stars Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Billy Magnussen, Bill Burr and Betty Gilpin.
The Social Reckoning hits theaters Friday.
Musk (Oct. 16)

The upcoming documentary Musk is by lauded filmmaker Alex Gibney, whose work includes Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.

Running about 4 hours, the movie delves into the life and legend of Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, and (cue Dr. Evil’s theme music) the richest man in the world. Given that the film seems to dismantle the mythos he built and sold along the way, Musk hasn’t had kind words to say, calling the movie a “hit piece” and Gibney a “douchebag” in a social media rant.

For a brief period, ads for the movie were barred from social media platforms Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X. Google and Meta have since cleared the way for promotional materials for Musk, while the other platforms have remained silent.
Musk hits theaters on Oct. 16 and will stream on HBO Max next year.
You Can See Everything (Oct. 16)

In case you’re unfamiliar with the story of Holmes, Gibney’s 2019 movie is a good place to start. You could also try the 2022 Hulu original series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried. Holmes, who was the face of Theranos, a short-lived blood-testing company, was indicted in June 2018 for fraud and conspiracy.

You Can See Everything is a nearly 3-hour-long documentary by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim (the director of the Chris Hanson drama Primetime), which appears more like a psychological horror film than a nonfiction narrative. The new movie follows Fielder into the private life of Holmes and her family, roughly a month before she was to report to prison. You Can See Everything has a hefty amount of buzz behind it and is turning into one of fall’s must-see theatrical releases.
You Can See Everything is released Oct. 16.
Artificial (Dec. 25)

Italian film director Luca Guadagnino (Call Me By Your Name and Queer) turns his eye on OpenAI’s Altman in his upcoming biopic, Artificial. Just like The Social Reckoning, this isn’t a documentary, and it’s already generating substantial Oscar buzz.

Artificial takes place in 2023 and follows the tumultuous period when Altman was fired by OpenAI and then rehired five days later. Amazon MGM Studios was originally set to distribute the movie, but after signing a multiyear partnership with OpenAI, it stepped away from the project. Neon came in and picked up the film, which also stars Billie Lourd, Monica Barbaro, Chris O’Dowd, Jason Schwartzman, Zozia Mamet and Ike Barinholtz (who plays Musk).
Artificial will premiere in theaters on Christmas Day.
What to stream
If you’re watching from home, you can also cash in on the Big Tech dystopia genre.

AMC’s The Audacity is a fictional account of the Silicon Valley tech bubble. Netflix has the documentary The AI Doc or How I Became an Apocaloptimist and will soon release AI Gone Wild, a new Instadoc about the rather infamous Hugging Face cyberattack. The streamer will also debut The Altruists, an eight-episode true-crime series about the 2022 collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s cryptocurrency empire, FTX, on Nov. 19. There’s even a legal procedural called Cupertino coming to CBS this week that is about Silicon Valley lawyers.

articles.headline: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay
keyFacts: South African legal pioneer Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for defending international law.
Pillay's career includes defending Nelson Mandela against apartheid and leading a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Despite turning 85 last month, Pillay stated that she has no intention of stopping her work.
body: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African legal pioneer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for defending international law and institutions in a world where increasingly “might overtakes right.”

Pillay, 85, has a decadeslong career that spans defending Nelson Mandela and standing up against the racist apartheid regime in South Africa, to leading a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
“Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said.
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay

Using the award to make a wider point about geopolitics, Frydnes contrasted Pillay’s work with the wider international “shift towards power politics,” in which “international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack.”

Her “distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law,” he said. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

Pillay learned of her prize at the Nuremberg Forum, an international law gathering in Germany. She told an applauding crowd, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” prompting laughter.

That was a reference to President Donald Trump’s longstanding ambitions to win the Peace Prize, and the offer by last year’s winner, Maria Corina Machado, to share it with him as she sought support for her efforts in Venezuela.
“Everybody asks me: ‘When are you going to stop? When are you going to stop?’” Pillay said, adding that despite turning 85 last month she had no intention of doing so.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza, namely what’s happening there is genocide,” she said to cheers.

“One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage,” she added. “But why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law and you look at all the facts.”
Having just been told the news, she added jokingly, “Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information.”
Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, was in Germany and among the first people to tell Pillay she had won.

“This could not be a better choice at a time of attacks against international justice,” Callamard told NBC News. “She is a former ICC judge at a time when the U.S. administration is seeking to destroy the ICC” and she led the U.N. commission, “which found that Israel committed the crime of genocide at a time when many states are trying to defend and protect Israel’s actions.”

Pillay was not among the pre-announcement frontrunners, who included Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of anti-Kremlin figure Alexei Navalny, Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate, and Mykola Kuleba, who founded an organization to rescue Ukrainian children abducted and forcibly deported by Russia.
Trump was among the 287 candidates, according to the leaders of Israel, Pakistan and Cambodia, who said they nominated him. But Trump said this week he didn’t think he would win.
“I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.”
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.headline: South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize
keyFacts: South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize for her lifetime commitment to international law.
Pillay's career includes defending anti-apartheid activists, serving as a UN High Commissioner, and ruling that rape can constitute an act of genocide.
The Nobel Peace Prize carries prize money of approximately 1.2 million dollars, and NPR stated this breaking story will be updated.
body: South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize
Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay, a leading South African jurist and former U.N. human rights chief, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her lifetime commitment to international law.
At a ceremony in Oslo, Norwegian Nobel Committee Chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes called Pillay "one of the most courageous and legal experts of our time."

"There is a thread to her involvement in standing and supporting Nelson Mandela and the prisoners of Robben Island, to her being a key to all the major international court cases of our time," he said.

Born in Durban in 1941, Pillay—who is a South African of Indian-Tamil descent—became the first woman of color to open a legal practice in her home province of Natal, where she defended anti-apartheid activists.
In 1973, she successfully sued the government to establish that political prisoners on South Africa's infamous Robben Island, including Nelson Mandela, had the right to legal representation.

A year after apartheid ended in 1994, Pillay became a high court judge in South Africa. She was shortly appointed to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, where she presided over a landmark case that established that rape and sexual assault could constitute an acts of genocide.
Pillay later served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, and later still, as a judge at the International Criminal Court.
The 85-year old was attending a conference in Nuremberg, Germany, when she received the news she had won the Nobel Peace Prize.

"If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she joked in front of a small crowd of well-wishers. "Being a lawyer and a judge I still want to verify this information," she added, to laughter.
Pillay referred to her recent work as the chair of the U.N. commission of inquiry, which concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
She also sought to play down suggestions that she was courageous.
"Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's impartial decision-making," she said.

This year's Nobel Peace Prize attracted 287 nominations, including individuals and organizations. The award carries prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately $1.2 million. The 2026 prize marks the 125th anniversary of the Nobel Peace Prize, first awarded in 1901.
This is a breaking story and will be updated.

articles.headline: Bucky Irving runs riot as Buccaneers stun Cowboys for first win of season
keyFacts: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers defeated the Dallas Cowboys 24-16 on Thursday night to secure their first win of the season.
Running back Bucky Irving rushed for 165 yards and scored two touchdowns, while rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels made his second career start.
Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield is expected to miss at least one more game with a dislocated thumb on his throwing hand.
body: Bucky Irving already had his first 100-yard game since his rookie year in 2024 when the Tampa Bay running back finished off the Dallas Cowboys with a run that gave him a career high.

Jalon Daniels, the undrafted rookie filling in for franchise quarterback Baker Mayfield, enjoyed the view while doing plenty himself to get the Buccaneers their first win of the season in just his second start.
Irving ran for 165 yards, including a 72-yard run to set up the touchdown that put Tampa Bay ahead for good while scoring twice himself, and the Buccaneers beat the Cowboys 24-16 on Thursday night.

Daniels threw a TD pass to Irving in the first half while directing a turnover-free offense and amid several Dallas miscues, finishing an efficient 19 of 25 for 189 yards as the Bucs piled up 241 yards rushing.
Daniels is filling in for Baker Mayfield, who’s expected to be sidelined at least one more game with a dislocated thumb on his throwing hand.

“Six months ago, if you would have told me that my first win would have been on a Thursday night, [Amazon] Prime football game, I don’t know what I would have told you,” said Daniels, who threw three interceptions in a 17-14 loss to Green Bay in his debut. “Like I keep saying, through all the highs and lows, the bads, the goods, go through every single emotion because at the end of the day, it makes you better and prepares you for any situation that comes down the line.”

Irving had 21 carries and a 7.9-yard average while scoring on a 5-yard pass and a 1-yard plunge as the Bucs (1-4) finally found some footing in a season that started with expectations of winning the NFC South.

“We lost the first quarter of the season,” Bucs coach Todd Bowles said. “We didn’t lose the second, third or fourth. We’ve still got to play those. So we started the second quarter tonight. It’s a long way to climb out, but at the same time, we’re upbeat and if we played as hard and played as effective, we’ll be OK.”

Dak Prescott led a 99-yard drive and threw a 13-yard TD pass to George Pickens in the fourth quarter before his second interception off a tipped pass helped Tampa Bay clinch the win in the final two minutes.
The Cowboys (2-3) continued an up-and-down start to the season, this time with an offense that was at times as sloppy as the defense has been in both seasons under coach Brian Schottenheimer.
“I didn’t plan on being 2-3, disappointed by that for sure,” Schottenheimer said. “But we’re just getting started. There’s a lot of football left and we’re gonna play better. We know that.”

After Irving’s long run on the first play of the second half was followed by receiver Emeka Egbuka’s 14-yard TD run on a jet sweep, Prescott threw his first interception and the Dallas defense left Tez Johnson wide open on a 64-yard grab that led to Irving’s 1-yard plunge for a 21-10 lead.
KaVontae Turpin’s fumble on the subsequent kickoff led to a Tampa Bay field goal, but only after the Bucs converted a third-and-21 from the Dallas 48-yard line with Daniels’ 21-yard pass to Egbuka.

The Cowboys were missing one of the pieces they recently added to try to fix a porous defense. Cornerback Joey Porter Jr was a late scratch in what was supposed to be his second appearance since arriving in a trade from Pittsburgh last week.
Prescott was 24 of 42 for 316 yards in his first two-interception game of the season – his first picks since the opener.

articles.headline: President Trump awards Big Tech donors with nation’s highest science prizes
keyFacts: President Trump awarded the National Medal of Science and the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to six Big Tech leaders.
The awardees have donated nearly six billion dollars to efforts tied to Trump and his administration, according to The New Republic.
Satya Nadella received his medal right after the administration indefinitely suspended Microsoft from the H-1B program for skilled foreign workers.
body: On Thursday, at the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit, President Trump awarded Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Sergey Brin, and AMD’s Lisa Su the National Medal of Science, the nation’s top science prize. Dell Technologies’ Michael Dell and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella also received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

Together, the awardees have donated nearly $6 billion to efforts tied to Trump and his administration, according to The New Republic. Alphabet and Microsoft, for example, donated to the president’s inauguration fund and White House ballroom. AMD gave to a pro-Trump Super PAC, and Michael and Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion to help fund the Trump Accounts, the administration’s savings program for children.
Trump said the honorees had helped “pioneer an incredible future for America,” and that because of them, “we will always be on top. No one else can compete with us.”
Nadella received his medal right after the administration indefinitely suspended Microsoft from the H-1B program, which lets U.S. companies hire skilled foreign workers.

articles.headline: SpaceX calls for better coordination in orbit after near-misses with Starlink
keyFacts: SpaceX executive Michael Nicolls called for improved data-sharing and coordination among satellite operators to prevent orbital collisions.
SpaceX's Starlink constellation currently operates over 11,000 satellites, representing about two-thirds of all active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit.
No global treaties or regulations currently require satellite operators to broadcast their locations or coordinate maneuvers in orbit.
body: Space has plenty of room for more megaconstellations, but only if all operators are willing to share information about where their satellites are and where they’re going, a top executive at SpaceX and its AI subsidiary said this week.

Michael Nicolls, SpaceX’s vice president for Starlink and president of Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, used a presentation Tuesday at the International Astronautical Congress in Turkey as a clarion call for improved data-sharing among satellite operators.

SpaceX’s Starlink constellation now has more than 11,000 satellites, about two-thirds of all active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit. Radars and telescopes routinely track thousands more pieces of space junk.

Starlink is, by far, the largest satellite constellation in operation today. But if you buy the buzz, Starlink is just the tip of the iceberg. SpaceX has revealed plans to launch up to a million satellites for a new constellation, called Starmind, to deploy AI computing capacity in low-Earth orbit. Amazon is in the early stages of launching a network of thousands of satellites to compete with Starlink, and two Chinese megaconstellations are now in full-scale deployment.
Law of large numbers

All of this raises the question of how to mitigate the risk of a collision in orbit, an event that could create thousands more pieces of space junk, potentially triggering a self-perpetuating cycle of debris generation. The risk of a collision on any given day is fantastically low. Space is vast and empty, and low-Earth orbit is a long way from filling up. SpaceX and most other Western operators de-orbit their rockets and satellites at the end of their missions to prevent additional debris in orbit.
“That said, the law of large numbers says that if it can happen, it will happen,” Nicolls said.

There’s still a long way to go to improve tracking, awareness, and coordination in orbit. This is sometimes called space traffic management. No global treaties or regulations require satellites to broadcast their locations and maneuvers or mandate coordination among satellite operators. Without rules of the road, it is up to governments and companies to set norms of behavior.
